task.description:
RE-GATE of the ISS-0440 design after rework 1 (commit adcfc591). You FAILED the prior revision on two BLOCKERs. Items 5 and 6 PASSED and are settled; the autofix refusal contract was verified correct and only its premise was wrong. Do not re-litigate any of that. This re-gate has three questions.

1. BLOCKER 1 -- IS THE OVERCLAIM ACTUALLY GONE, AND IS WHAT REPLACED IT TRUE? CODE-DESIGNER reports it WITHDREW the claim rather than softening it: new section 0 distinguishes two reliability classes, section 1.2 states plainly that HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.3 is prose ORCH executes rather than code-enforced, and new section 3.5 concludes that ONLY Mechanism A carries the structural guarantee -- if B were silently dropped, A still catches every violation at CI before merge, so B is a latency win on the common path, not a second independent guarantee. ORCH grepped the file: the surviving 'structurally impossible' strings are the design correcting itself (line 81 quotes the withdrawn claim, 110 says the word is earned by Mechanism A alone, 381 supplies the corrected sentence). VERIFY the reframing is complete and internally consistent -- no section still argues from the withdrawn premise -- AND, more importantly, judge whether the NEW claim is itself true: does Mechanism A genuinely catch 100% of these at CI before merge? Consider the admin-override path specifically: a maintainer CAN merge past a red CI check (ORCH did exactly that on PR #848 hours ago, for an unrelated documented flake). If admin override can bypass A, then A is not absolutely unavoidable either, and the design should say so rather than repeating the same class of overclaim one level down. This is the item most likely to hide a second-order version of the defect you already caught once.

2. BLOCKER 2 -- DOES THE AC1 DEMONSTRATION NOW EXECUTE? The design adds a `--dir <path>` flag to run/1 threading into handoff_files/1's existing dir parameter, with resolve_dir/1 returning @handoffs_dir when the flag is absent. Verify: (i) the design's specified no-flag behaviour is genuinely byte-identical to today's CI invocation (CI passes no args at all -- confirm from .github/workflows/ci.yml and mix.exs); (ii) the rewritten section 5 demonstration is now actually executable by a real CLI run -- plant PASS, catch it; --autofix, correct it; plant FAIL, refuse it; confirm the no-flag path still scans only the real corpus; (iii) the inside-handoffs/ fixture alternative is rejected with the cross-host-CI-breakage hazard named. Note the design cannot be proven to execute until ELIXIR-DEV builds it -- your job is to confirm the PLAN is now mechanically coherent against the real source, not to run it.

3. NEW RISK INTRODUCED BY THE FIX ITSELF -- assess this even though it is not in the original six items. A --dir flag on a linter that is a HARD CI GATE is new attack surface for accidental misuse: someone could run `mix letflow.lint_handoffs --dir some/empty/dir`, get a clean 0-violation result, and believe the corpus is clean. Judge whether the design guards against that or should. Consider whether --dir should refuse a directory containing zero discovered files, or emit a loud banner naming the scanned directory and file count, so a scoped run can never be mistaken for a full one. Also confirm --autofix combined with --dir cannot be pointed at the real corpus to mass-rewrite it in a way nobody reviews -- state what the design says happens there.

BIAS TOWARD CLOSING: rework 1 of max 3. If the reframing is honest, the demonstration is coherent, and item 3 is either guarded or explicitly accepted with reasoning, PASS it. Do not hold the gate for wording preferences. If you FAIL, be exhaustive and precise so rework 2 is mechanical.

Do not edit lib/ or test/. Complete the handoff with per-item verdicts and a clear PASS/FAIL; on PASS route to ELIXIR-DEV. Commit to branch feature/WF03-ISS0440-20260903.

result.summary: FAIL. Re-gate after rework 1 (design commit adcfc591). Read the revised lib/letflow/design/iss440-handoff-status-enforcement.md directly, plus lib/mix/tasks/letflow.lint_handoffs.ex, .github/workflows/ci.yml, mix.exs. Items 5 and 6 not re-litigated per instruction. One BLOCKER (Item 1, second-order recurrence of the overclaim defect) plus a second BLOCKER (Item 3, unguarded new misuse surface).  ITEM 1 -- FAIL. The withdrawal of the first overclaim is real and internally consistent: grepped the whole file for structurally-impossible / 100% / no-path-through phrasing -- the surviving instance at line 81 is explicitly quoted as the withdrawn claim (the design says plainly that claim is not literally true and is withdrawn), and sections 1.2/3.5/AC1 correctly scope the word to Mechanism A alone rather than the pair. So the FIRST-order fix is genuine, not cosmetic. BUT the task named this as the item most likely to hide a second-order version of the same defect, and it does: section 3.5 states that if Mechanism B were silently dropped, the violation would still be caught every time by Mechanism A at CI, before merge, and that nothing about structurally-impossible-to-merge depends on B -- and AC1 repeats it, calling merge-blocking literally true because nothing bypasses CI. Independently verified this is FALSE as stated, not merely imprecise: gh api repos/tvolodi/letflow/branches/main/protection returns 404 Branch not protected -- main carries zero required status checks, zero merge restrictions. And PR #848's own statusCheckRollup (gh pr view 848 --json statusCheckRollup), merged 2026-09-03T06:46:19Z, shows one of its two Backend gate check runs completed with conclusion FAILURE at merge time -- a real, contemporaneous counterexample sitting in this repo's own history, not a hypothetical. So Mechanism A's actual guarantee is narrower than the design's central claim: CI runs unconditionally and DETECTS the violation unconditionally (that part is true and structural -- ci.yml:126 is a bare, unconditional mix letflow.check invocation, no if: or continue-on-error), but CI BLOCKING A MERGE is not structurally enforced by GitHub in this repo's current configuration -- it depends on the merging agent choosing to honor a red or incomplete check, which is the same procedural character as the section-1.3 claim this rework just withdrew one level up. The design's structurally-impossible-to-merge sentence needs the same correction its predecessor got: this is a second occurrence of the exact defect class the gate exists to catch, one level down, and cannot be waved through as a wording preference -- it is the design's one remaining claim to a structural (not merely procedural) guarantee, and that claim does not hold against this repo's actual configuration. Required correction: state a third tier explicitly -- CI running and recording a violation is structural and unconditional; a red or incomplete CI check actually blocking a merge is procedural (depends on the merging agent honoring the result, exactly like Mechanism B / section 1.3), because main carries no branch protection. The honest AC1 answer becomes unconditional detection, always, plus two procedural enforcement/early-catch layers (A's block-on-honor and B's pre-commit read) with independent, currently-clean track records -- not structurally impossible to merge. A repo-level branch-protection change would be the genuine structural fix for the merge-blocking half, but that is repo-administration scope outside ISS-0440's affected_files and would affect every concurrent run on every host -- recommended as a follow-up issue, not a requirement of this design.  ITEM 2 -- PASS. Confirmed against current source: ci.yml:126 is a bare mix letflow.check invocation with no arguments; mix.exs's letflow.check alias still calls the bare string letflow.lint_handoffs, no arguments appended -- both unchanged, matching section 2.1's claim that CI's invocation is untouched. handoff_files/1 (lib/mix/tasks/ letflow.lint_handoffs.ex around lines 277-279, current source, pre-ELIXIR-DEV) already has the dir-with-default-@handoffs_dir parameter the design's --dir plan threads into -- the capability genuinely exists one layer down and is simply unreachable from the CLI today, exactly as claimed. The design's resolve_dir/1 spec (no flag maps to @handoffs_dir, matching CI's own empty-args resolution byte for byte) is mechanically coherent against this signature. The rewritten section 5 demonstration (plant PASS outside handoffs/, run --dir against a fixture to catch; --autofix to fix; plant FAIL to refuse; confirm the no-flag path is unaffected) is now genuinely executable once ELIXIR-DEV wires the two flags -- no mechanical gap found, unlike rework 0's version. The inside-handoffs/ fixture alternative is explicitly named and rejected with the cross-host-CI-breakage hazard stated verbatim (section 5 step 6's closing paragraph explains a bad-status file left inside handoffs/ would be linted by every other host's mix letflow.check and would break their builds the moment it is committed). No defects found on this item.  ITEM 3 -- FAIL, unguarded. Grepped the design for any handling of an empty-result --dir invocation or an --autofix-plus-dir-at-real-corpus combination: neither is addressed. (a) Empty-directory misuse: resolve_dir/1's only stated error case is a missing flag VALUE; nothing in the design covers a --dir pointed at a directory that resolves but discovers zero step-prefixed files. As specified, that run would print a clean OK result over zero handoff files and exit 0 -- functionally indistinguishable at the exit-code level, and easy to misread at the text level, from a genuinely clean full-corpus run. This is exactly the misuse the task named: someone runs --dir against an empty or wrong directory, gets a clean result, and wrongly believes the corpus is clean. The design should either specify that zero discovered files is itself flagged (a loud banner naming the scanned directory and file count, or a non-zero exit or explicit warning on zero-file runs) so a scoped run can never be silently mistaken for a full one. (b) --autofix plus --dir pointed at the real corpus: --dir is specified as unrestricted (section 2.1's only validation named is that the flag has a following argument) -- nothing in the design prevents pointing --dir back at the real handoffs directory together with --autofix, which per sections 2.2-2.4 would run the full corrective rewrite path over the entire real corpus, live, locally, unreviewed. The design is silent on this combination throughout -- grepped for autofix/dir co-occurrence and for any mass-rewrite/real-corpus caveat; found none. Today's corpus has zero live H1 violations (confirmed this session and the prior gate), so the immediate blast radius is near zero, but the design introduces this surface without discussion, and a future corpus state could differ. Required correction: the design must either state explicitly that --autofix run against the real handoffs/ directory (whether via the default or via an explicit --dir) is an accepted, intended local-developer capability with reasoning for why unreviewed mass-rewrite of production handoff files is safe (e.g. because the mapping is a closed, verified-safe 3-value set per section 2.2, and refused/ambiguous files are never touched), or add a guard (e.g. require an explicit confirmation flag, or restrict --autofix to apply only when --dir also names a non-default directory, forcing the real corpus through the plain non-autofix CI path only). Either is acceptable; silence is not.  VERDICT: FAIL. Two BLOCKERs (Item 1's second-order overclaim recurrence, Item 3's unguarded --dir misuse surface). Item 2 passes cleanly with no defects. Route back to CODE-DESIGNER; this is not a wording preference -- Item 1 in particular is the exact failure class this gate exists to catch, and the task explicitly flagged it as the item most likely to hide a recurrence, which it does.

issues.description: Item 1: design section 3.5 and AC1 claim the violation is structurally impossible to merge because nothing bypasses CI, and that if Mechanism B were silently dropped the violation would still be caught every time by Mechanism A at CI, before merge. Verified independently and found FALSE as currently configured: gh api repos/tvolodi/letflow/branches/main/ protection returns 404 Branch not protected -- main has zero required status checks or merge restrictions. gh pr view 848 --json statusCheckRollup shows PR #848 (merged 2026-09-03T06:46:19Z) had one of its two Backend gate check runs complete with conclusion FAILURE at merge time -- a real counterexample in this repo's own recent history. CI running and detecting the violation IS structural and unconditional (ci.yml:126, a bare mix letflow.check invocation, no if: or continue-on-error) -- that much of the claim holds. But CI BLOCKING a merge is not structurally enforced by GitHub here; it depends on the merging agent choosing to honor a red or incomplete check, the same procedural character as the section-1.3 claim withdrawn earlier in this same rework. This is a second occurrence of the exact overclaim defect one level down, in the design's one remaining claim to a structural (not merely procedural) guarantee. Rework: replace the structurally-impossible- to-merge framing in section 3.5 and AC1 with an honest three-tier statement -- (i) CI detection is structural and unconditional; (ii) CI blocking an actual merge is procedural, resting on the merging agent honoring the result, because main carries no branch protection; (iii) Mechanism B's pre-commit read is also procedural, per the already- corrected section 1.2/3.5 text. State plainly that no tier of this design provides an unconditional merge-block guarantee in this repo's current configuration -- only unconditional detection. A repo-level branch-protection change (requiring the Backend gate check to pass before merge) would supply the missing structural merge-block guarantee but is out of this design's affected_files/scope and would affect every concurrent run on every host -- record it as a recommended follow-up issue, not a requirement of this design.

Item 3: the design does not guard against, or even acknowledge, two new misuse paths its own --dir flag introduces on a hard CI-gate linter. (a) A --dir pointed at a directory with zero discovered step-prefixed files runs cleanly to an OK result over zero handoff files and exit 0, textually and structurally similar to a genuinely clean full-corpus run -- nothing in resolve_dir/1's spec (section 2.1) or elsewhere addresses this; the design only specifies an error for a missing flag VALUE, not for a valid-but-empty or wrong directory. Someone running the linter with --dir against a wrong directory could reasonably believe the real corpus was checked when it was not. (b) --autofix combined with --dir pointed at the real corpus (or simply --autofix alone against the default) is unrestricted per section 2.1's spec and would run the full corrective rewrite over every real handoff file matching the closed autofix map, live and unreviewed -- the design never discusses this combination anywhere (grepped for co-occurrence, found none). Rework: either (i) specify that a zero-file discovery result under --dir prints a loud, distinct banner naming the scanned directory and the file count (so a scoped or empty run can never be mistaken for a full one) rather than reusing the same OK message as a real clean run, and/or a non-zero exit or explicit warning in that case; and (ii) explicitly state whether --autofix against the real corpus (default dir or an explicit --dir naming it) is an accepted, intended capability -- with reasoning for why unreviewed mass-rewrite of production handoff files is safe given the closed 3-value map -- or add a guard restricting it. Silence on either point is not acceptable for a flag added to a hard CI gate every in-flight run on every host depends on.

result.next_action: Rework CODE-DESIGNER -- 2 BLOCKERs (Item 1 second-order overclaim, Item 3 unguarded --dir misuse surface) named above; Item 2 passed cleanly, do not re-litigate. Rework iteration 2 of 3.
